## Purpose of This Page

This page defines the foundation of our career-evaluation product. It explains who the product is designed for, what career question it will answer, and why Computer Systems Design and Related Services is a relevant industry for analytics careers.
:::

## 1. Career Pathway

<!-- SECTION OWNER: Entire team -->
<!-- INSTRUCTIONS: Select one career pathway related to analytics, business intelligence, data science, machine learning, or data engineering. -->

**Selected career pathway:** Data Analytics

**Why we selected it:**
Data Analytics was selected because it represents a broad and practical career pathway that appears across many technology-driven organizations. It also allows the team to evaluate multiple related role types while focusing on the skills, qualifications, compensation, and market conditions most relevant to aspiring analytics professionals.

## 2. Industry Selection

<!-- SECTION OWNER: Jenna -->
<!-- INSTRUCTIONS: Explain why NAICS 5415 is relevant to the selected analytics career pathway. -->

**Selected industry:** Computer Systems Design and Related Services
**NAICS code:** 5415

### Industry Justification

Computer Systems Design and Related Services is highly relevant to the Data Analytics career pathway because organizations in this industry rely heavily on data, software, information systems, and technology-enabled decision-making. The course dataset also provides a substantially larger analytical sample for this industry, supporting more meaningful analysis of labor-market patterns.

### Role of Analytics in This Industry

Analytics professionals in this industry support areas such as business intelligence, data analysis, systems performance, technology consulting, reporting, forecasting, and data-driven decision-making. These roles may require candidates to interpret large datasets, identify trends, build reports and dashboards, and translate analytical findings into recommendations for clients or internal business teams.

## 3. Target User

<!-- SECTION OWNER: Mariam  -->
<!-- INSTRUCTIONS: Describe the type of student or job seeker who would use this career-evaluation product. -->

### User Profile

The target user is a student, recent graduate, or early-career professional interested in pursuing an analytics-related career within the Computer Systems Design and Related Services industry. The user may have foundational experience with data analysis, statistics, business analytics, or related disciplines and some exposure to tools such as Excel, SQL, Python, R, or data visualization platforms. However, they may have limited professional experience in technology-focused organizations and may not yet understand how their existing skills align with available analytics roles.

### User Needs

Before applying for analytics positions in Computer Systems Design and Related Services, the target user needs a clearer understanding of the types of analytics roles available, the technical and professional skills employers commonly request, typical education requirements, salary expectations, geographic and remote work patterns, and potential skill gaps. This information can help the user evaluate their current qualifications and identify which skills or experiences they should prioritize to become a more competitive candidate.

## 4. Product Question

<!-- SECTION OWNER: Entire team -->
<!-- INSTRUCTIONS: Agree on one primary product question and supporting analytical questions. -->

### Primary Question

> How can an aspiring analytics professional evaluate career opportunities in Computer Systems Design and Related Services and determine which skills, qualifications, and experiences to prioritize to become a competitive candidate?

### Supporting Questions

1. What analytics roles appear most frequently in Computer Systems Design and Related Services?
2. Which technical and professional skills are most commonly requested?
3. How do salary, experience, location, and remote-work patterns vary?
4. Where does the target user have skill gaps?
5. Which skills should the target user prioritize?

<!-- EDITING NOTE: Revise or replace these supporting questions after the team selects its primary focus area. -->

## 5. Project Rationale

<!-- SECTION OWNER: Mariam -->
<!-- INSTRUCTIONS: Explain the problem, why it matters, and how the finished product will help its intended user. -->

### Problem Statement

Students and early-career professionals may not have a clear understanding of the skills and job-market needs required for analytics roles within Computer Systems Design and Related Services, which can result in difficulty identifying appropriate roles and determining how well their qualifications align with employer expectations.

### Why the Question Matters

Understanding these requirements is important because students and early-career professionals may need more than general analytics knowledge when preparing for a career in a specific industry. Knowing which skills, qualifications, and experience employers are seeking can help job seekers make more informed decisions about their career preparation and identify areas they may need to develop before applying. It also enables them to better communicate their own skill sets to align with market needs.

### Value of the Product

The finished product will provide job seekers with the insights and information needed to better position themselves in the job market, assess their skills and identify areas for self-improvement, and better communicate their strengths based on what employers are seeking. By bringing together information about available roles, required skills and qualifications, salary, location, and work arrangements, the product can support users in their job search and help them better understand current market needs.

## 6. Literature Review

### Source 1: NAICS 5415 Industry Definition

**Citation:** U.S. Census Bureau. (2022). *2022 NAICS definition: Computer Systems Design and Related Services (5415).*

**Summary and relevance:** The U.S. Census Bureau defines NAICS 5415 as establishments that provide computer systems design and related services. This includes work involving computer hardware, software, and communication technologies [@census2022naics5415]. The definition helps keep our analysis focused on the industry selected by the team.

### Source 2: Data Scientist Career Profile

**Citation:** O\*NET OnLine. (2026). *Data Scientists, 15-2051.00.*

**Summary and relevance:** O\*NET describes Data Scientists as professionals who turn raw data into useful information through programming, visualization, data mining, modeling, and related methods [@onet2026datascientists]. It also lists tasks such as preparing data, creating charts, explaining results, and recommending data-based solutions. This supports our decision to study several connected analytics roles rather than one exact job title.

### Source 3: Skills in Analytics Job Advertisements

**Citation:** Verma, A., Yurov, K. M., Lane, P. L., & Yurova, Y. V. (2019). An investigation of skill requirements for business and data analytics positions: A content analysis of job advertisements. *Journal of Education for Business, 94*(4), 243–250.

**Summary and relevance:** This study compares the skills requested for Business Analyst, Data Analyst, and Data Scientist positions [@verma2019skills]. It shows that the roles share some skills but also have important differences. This supports the use of job postings to compare related career paths and explains why we grouped several analytics titles while still reporting separate occupation categories.

## 7. Expected Dataset Fields

<!-- SECTION OWNER: Sebastian -->

The table below lists the main fields used in the project and what each field supports.

| Field or Variable | How the Team Uses It |
|---|---|
| Industry or NAICS code | Filter postings to NAICS 5415, Computer Systems Design and Related Services |
| Job title | Identify which analytics roles appear and group them into a role family |
| Company or employer | Check how concentrated hiring is across employers in Computer Systems Design and Related Services |
| Skills | Primary input to the skill-gap analysis; rank the tools and competencies employers request |
| Software or specialized skills | Separate tool requirements such as SQL, Python, R, Tableau, and Power BI from general competencies |
| Certifications | Identify professional or technical credentials included in analytics postings |
| Experience (minimum and maximum years) | Judge which roles are realistic for an early-career candidate |
| Education level | Record degree expectations, which we expect to run higher in this industry than in analytics generally |
| Salary (minimum and maximum) | Describe advertised compensation ranges for the selected analytics roles |
| City, state, and metropolitan area | Map where analytics opportunities are geographically concentrated |
| Remote-work status | Compare remote, hybrid, and onsite postings |
| Posting date and duration | Confirm the postings are recent and check whether the sample is spread evenly over time |

### Note on Data Volume

The original NAICS 3254 industry scope produced too few relevant analytics postings to support meaningful distribution-level analysis. In Module 2, the team therefore revised the industry scope to NAICS 5415, Computer Systems Design and Related Services. In Module 3 the panel was rebuilt on the corrected v2 extract and limited to the most recent 12 months of postings, as documented on the [Data Preparation](data_cleaning.qmd) page. This provides a stronger basis for evaluating salary, geography, education, work arrangements, employers, and other labor-market patterns.

## 8. What We Expect to Explore

<!-- SECTION OWNER: Drafted by Sebastian, pending team review -->

Within Computer Systems Design and Related Services, we expect analytics opportunities to span several related role types and employer contexts. Our analysis will examine how demand varies across job titles, employers, salary levels, education requirements, geographic markets, and work arrangements. We will also evaluate the skills information available in the dataset while documenting limitations in the source data rather than assuming that missing skills or experience fields represent employer preferences. These expectations will be tested against the data and revised where the evidence supports a different conclusion.

### Not Included

- Careers unrelated to the selected pathway
